column1: Why are LUFS (loudness) and True Peak considered orthogonal measurements rather than two views of the same thing?
column2: LUFS measures perceived loudness over time (how loud something sounds to a human), while True Peak measures instantaneous proximity to the digital ceiling (overload risk). A signal can be high in one and low in the other; satisfying one does not satisfy the other.

column1: What is the integration time constant of a classic VU meter, and what effect does this have on reading transient-heavy material?
column2: 300 ms. This slow ballistic response acts like an analog low-pass filter on signal energy, causing VU meters to under-report fast transients and make mixes look softer/more 'musically alive' than they technically are.

column1: What problem did Peak Program Meters (PPM) solve that VU meters could not?
column2: PPMs use fast attack times (a few milliseconds) to catch transient peaks that slow-responding VU meters miss due to mechanical/ballistic inertia, protecting transmission and recording chains from clipping.

column1: What historical phenomenon drove the development of ITU-R BS.1770 / EBU R128 loudness standards?
column2: The 'loudness war': simple peak normalization let producers use dynamic range compression to sound louder than competitors without raising peak amplitude, so loudness-perception-based metering (LUFS) was created to standardize fair comparison.

column1: What is the core invariant distinguishing mastering EQ moves from mixing EQ moves?
column2: Mastering EQ is corrective, not additive: every move must address a measured/perceived deviation from a reference target curve on the full summed stereo signal, since any boost/cut affects every instrument simultaneously (global 'blast radius').

column1: Why does A/B comparison against reference commercial tracks work better than soloed absolute judgment when tonal balancing?
column2: The ear is a poor absolute measuring instrument but an excellent comparative (null) detector—perception of brightness/balance drifts with fatigue, monitor volume, and room response, so comparing against loudness-matched references isolates true spectral differences.

column1: In a compressor, what does a 4:1 ratio mean numerically?
column2: For every 4 dB the input signal rises above the threshold, the output level increases by only 1 dB.

column1: How does mastering 'glue' compression create the perception of increased loudness without raising peak level?
column2: Human hearing integrates energy over ~200ms windows (temporal integration). Compression reduces variance in energy across these windows, raising the average energy perceived even though peak amplitude is unchanged.

column1: What three invariants must a mastering compression chain preserve to avoid damaging artistic intent? (first one given)
column2: Transient integrity (preserving percussive attacks/onsets) is the first; the text indicates two more follow (stereo image integrity and spectral balance are the typical remaining invariants in this framework).

column1: Why can't a naive sample-by-sample clipper at the Nyquist rate prevent all overs on playback?
column2: It cannot detect intersample peaks—excursions in the continuous-time reconstructed analog waveform between discrete samples—which can exceed digital sample magnitudes by 2–4 dB in transient-rich material.

column1: What are the two fundamental architectural approaches a brickwall limiter uses to catch intersample peaks?
column2: 1) Time-domain lookahead buffering: delays output while scanning future samples for peaks. 2) Frequency-domain oversampling: upsamples 2x/4x/8x to reveal intersample peaks as discrete samples that can be directly attenuated.

column1: At 48 kHz sample rate, how many milliseconds does a 96-sample plugin latency equal, and why does this matter in mastering?
column2: 96 samples / 48,000 samples per second = 2 ms. This is perceptually significant for mastering material with tight transients (e.g., jazz drum brushes, string pizzicato), since accumulated plugin latency can smear transient timing.
